deep.reconstruction:
This page has no mathematical derivation. It is the opening of a historical introduction to a lecture course on number theory, probably Riemann's own lecture notes. It continues onto the next page, which says the Disquisitiones is 'so compressed that it is hardly understood' and then begins elementary definitions such as multiplication. It has nothing to do with the optics/ether variational sketch on the previous page.

Content in order:

(1) Antiquity. Plato, Euclid and Diophantus. Diophantus is dated to the 3rd or 4th century ('sec. 3 od 4'), and his work is noted as not completely preserved ('nicht vollständig'). Of the 13 books of the Arithmetica, 6 were then known in Greek.

(2) Fermat. The real beginning of the subject is placed in the 17th century with Fermat, 'Parlamentsrath in Toulouse'. Fermat published little, and his results survived chiefly as marginal notes ('Randnoten') in his copy of Bachet's edition of Diophantus. These were published by his son, Samuel de Fermat, in 1670.

(3) Fermat's proofs. Fermat claims to have proofs for all his assertions. Riemann reports a conjecture that Fermat found some of them only by induction. He rejects the idea that so great a mind would hold to such claims without grounds: at least Fermat would not have believed he had proofs [reading uncertain].

(4) Euler. The Fermat theorems long resisted proof. Only around the middle of the 18th century ('des vorigen Jahrhunderts') did Euler begin to prove them. After years of effort ('40j.' as transcribed) Euler proved Fermat's theorem: every prime 4n+1 can always be written as a sum of two squares, and in only one way.

(5) After Euler. Lagrange, then Legendre, then Gauss, who with admirable success presented number theory as a connected whole in the Disquisitiones Arithmeticae (1801).

In modern terms, the single mathematical statement on the page is Fermat's two-squares theorem with uniqueness. For a prime p with p ≡ 1 (mod 4) there exist integers a > b > 0 with p = a^2 + b^2. This pair is unique up to order and signs. No proof or computation is given.
errors: 'Nach 40j. Anstrengungen' is historically inaccurate if read literally. Euler took up the two-squares problem around 1742 (correspondence with Goldbach). He sent a proof in 1749 (published 1752/1755), with the uniqueness argument also by Euler. That is roughly 7 years, not 40. Either the numeral is misread (possibly '7j.') or it is a lecture exaggeration. Forty years would fit Euler's whole career on Fermat's theorems.
Calling Fermat's death a 'frühen Tod' (early death), if the reading is right, is doubtful: Fermat died in 1665 aged about 57–64.

The claim that Fermat had proofs of all his assertions is presented as Fermat's own claim, and Riemann treats it critically. That is fair, since some claims were false, e.g. that all Fermat numbers are prime.

results.what: Every prime p ≡ 1 (mod 4) is a sum of two squares, and uniquely so (up to order and sign). Stated historically, without proof.
results.modern_name: Fermat's theorem on sums of two squares (Fermat–Euler two-squares theorem)
results.usually_credited_to: Stated by Fermat (1640, letter to Mersenne); first proof published by Euler (1752/1755, letter to Goldbach 1749)

results.what: Historical sketch of number theory: Diophantus, Fermat's marginal notes in Bachet's Diophantus, Euler, Lagrange, Legendre, Gauss's Disquisitiones Arithmeticae
results.modern_name: History of elementary number theory (lecture introduction)

deep.surprise_reason: These are standard lecture-introduction remarks on the history of number theory, as known to any mid-19th-century mathematician. There is no new mathematics. The only mildly interesting points are biographical: it is evidence of a Riemann number-theory lecture course, and of his sceptical but respectful view of Fermat's claimed proofs.

checkable.sympy: all(len([(a,b) for a in range(1,int(p**0.5)+1) for b in range(a,int(p**0.5)+1) if a**2+b**2==p])==1 for p in primerange(3,2000) if p%4==1)
checkable.asserts: Every prime p ≡ 1 mod 4 below 2000 has exactly one representation p = a^2 + b^2 with 0 < a ≤ b.

checkable.sympy: all(len([(a,b) for a in range(0,int(p**0.5)+1) for b in range(a,int(p**0.5)+1) if a**2+b**2==p])==0 for p in primerange(3,2000) if p%4==3)
checkable.asserts: No prime p ≡ 3 mod 4 is a sum of two squares (the complementary 'only' part).

transcription_corrections: Line 1: 'Diophant sei 3 od 4 nicht vollständig' is better read as 'Diophant sec. 3 od 4' (saeculum 3 or 4, i.e. 3rd/4th century) followed by '[Werk] nicht vollständig [erhalten]'.
Line 3–4: 'Ursprung [?]' is likely 'Anfang'. 'hauptsächl. [?] durch die Beschäf-' should read 'Fermat, Parlamentsrath in Toulouse'.

Lines 5–7: the fragment probably reads roughly 'durch frühen Tod an Vollendung ... seiner Schriften ... (by his son) ... herausgegeben/verloren'. 'Schwester [?]' and 'Druck [?]' are doubtful, and 'Sohn' fits the history (Samuel de Fermat, 1670 edition).
'Dass, dass er für alle Behauptungen' is likely 'Sagt, dass er für alle Behauptungen Beweise besitze'.
'meist [?] nur durch Induction' is possibly 'einige nur durch Induction'.
'Die meisten [?] ... die Fermat'schen Lehrsätze' is uncertain; the sense is that the Fermat theorems long occupied/resisted mathematicians.
'Nach 40j.' should be checked against the image; '7j.' would fit the history better.
Last line: 'zusammenhängend' continues on the next page as '... [zusammenhängend] dargestellt'.
